Types and type variables

We start by introducing the abstract syntax of types.

The type typ of mini-ML types is mutually recursive with the type tvar of type variables. Indeed, a type variable contains a possible definition (obtained during unification), which is itself a type. Thus { id = 1; def = None } is "still" a type variable, whereas { id = 2; def = Some Tint } is a former type variable that has been defined to be equal to the type Tint and must now be treated exactly as if it were the type Tint.

Concept: mutually recursive types

type … and … defines the two types together, so each can mention the other. Defined one after the other, the first would mention a type that does not exist yet.

Concept: mutable field of type option

A field declared mutable is changed in place by <-; the other fields never change.

The type typ option has two forms: None, no type yet, and Some t, the type t.

To test, we can use the following pretty-printing function:

Notion: printers of the module Format

The three printers call one another, so they are defined together by let rec … and ….

In a format, %a takes two arguments, a printer and the value to print; @. ends the line. @[<h> and @] open and close a box that keeps its content on one line.

We then introduce a module V encapsulating the type tvar with a comparison function and a function that creates a fresh type variable.

Concept: module and counter kept by a closure

A module groups a type and its functions; outside it, a name is written with the module in front, V.create.

The counter r is created once. The function fun () -> … keeps it, and nothing else can reach it: each call returns a variable with a new id.

Question 1. Normalization

To make handling type variables easier, we introduce two functions that normalize a type expression by following the definitions contained in type variables.

Write a function

that normalizes a type at the head, i.e., head t returns a type equal to t that is not of the form Tvar { def = Some _}. In other words, head t follows type-variable definitions at the head of t for as long as there are any.

Write a function

that completely normalizes a type, i.e., that applies the function head above recursively. This second function will be used only for printing types (in the result of a typing operation or in error messages).

Hint: normalization before every inspection

A defined variable is not a shape of its own: a variable whose field def is Some Tint has to be read as Tint. A function that matches on a type without calling head first takes it for a variable.

head is enough to look at the root of a type. canon rebuilds the whole type, and serves only to print a result or to compare it in a test.

Concept: failwith and the holes of the file

failwith msg raises the exception Failure msg. Like raise, it never returns and has any type, so it can stand for a body that is not written yet: the definition of a function is accepted, and fails only when the function is called. A value defined by a hole, as empty in question 4, fails at its definition.

Notion: record pattern with fields left out

The pattern Tvar { def = Some t } matches a defined variable whatever its id: a record pattern names only the fields it needs.

We can test with

Concept: test block and assert

let () = e evaluates e for its effect. assert c does nothing when c is true, and raises Assert_failure with the file, the line and the column when it is false.

In a tab of the Playground, the first assertion that fails stops everything after it.

Definition: structural and physical equality

= compares two values by their content. == holds when the two are the same object in memory: on a record with a mutable field, changing one changes the other.

The test head ta == ta asks head to return its argument itself, not a copy.

Question 2. Unification

To report unification errors, we use the following exception and function:

Write a function

Concept: exception with arguments

An exception is declared like a constructor, raised by raise, and caught by try … with, which matches on it.

raise e never returns, so it has any type: unification_error has type typ -> typ -> 'a, and a call is accepted where unify expects unit.

that tests whether a type variable occurs in a type (occur-check). We may assume that the variable itself is undefined. The type, however, may contain defined variables, and head should be applied to it before inspecting it.

Write a function

Hint: the cyclic type that the occur check prevents

Unifying α with α → int would write the definition α := α → int: a type that contains itself. canon, occur and fvars would then never finish on it.

The check comes before the definition is written. It is what rejects fun x -> x x.

performing the unification of two types. Again, head should be used on the argument types before they are inspected.

Hint: unification by assignment

unify returns unit: its result is the assignment v.def <- Some t, which every type built earlier with v then sees. No substitution is built or returned.

After head on both types, the cases are: Tint twice (nothing to do); the same variable twice (nothing to do, and never α := α); a variable and another type; two arrows or two products, component by component; anything else is a failure.

Concept: sequence, and if without else

e1; e2 evaluates e1, which should have type unit (the compiler warns otherwise), then e2, and has the value of e2. if c then e without else is accepted only when e has type unit, and does nothing when c is false.

The conditional ends at the semicolon: in if c then e1; e2 the expression e2 is evaluated whatever c is.

Concept: match on a pair, with a guard

match e1, e2 with looks at two values at once. A guard, when c, adds a condition to a case. Two patterns separated by | share a branch when they bind the same names.

We can test with

Notion: exception turned into a boolean

cant_unify answers true when unify raises UnificationFailure, and false when it returns. The tests can then assert that two types do not unify.

Question 3. Free variables of a type

To represent the set of free variables of a type, we use Caml's Set module.

Write a function

that computes the set of free variables of a type. Once again, we should use the function head appropriately so as to consider only variables that are not defined.

We can test with

Concept: functor Set.Make and the operations used

Set.Make is a functor: a function from modules to modules. Its argument is a module with a type t and a function compare, as V is, and its result is a module of sets of such values.

A set is immutable: Vset.add and Vset.union return a set and leave their arguments unchanged. Vset.fold f s init calls f on each element, with the result built so far.

Question 4. Typing environment

We define the following Caml type for type schemes:

Hint: type and type scheme

A scheme is a type with some of its variables quantified. The scheme ∀α. α → α is the record with vars = {α} and typ = α → α. A scheme whose set vars is empty is an ordinary type.

A quantified variable can be replaced by any type at each use; a variable that is not quantified is one unknown type, the same everywhere.

We then introduce dictionaries using strings as keys

and then the following Caml type for typing environments:

Concept: Map.Make, compared with a hash table

Smap is immutable: Smap.add returns a dictionary with the entry and leaves the old one unchanged, still valid. That gives scope for free: the environment extended for the body of a fun or a let is not seen outside it. Hashtbl.add changes the table in place, and the entry would have to be removed on the way out.

The keys are ordered by String.compare, not hashed, and Smap.find takes logarithmic time. It raises Not_found for an absent key.

The first field, bindings, contains the entries of the typing environment. The second, fvars, contains the set of all free type variables in the entries of bindings. The field fvars is only there to avoid recomputing the set of free variables of the environment every time generalization is performed. Note: some of these variables may become defined between the time they are added to this set and the time it is used. We must therefore update this set before using it (for example by applying fvars (Tvar v) to each variable v and taking the union of the results).

which adds an entry to a typing environment without generalization (it will be used for typing a function). Do not forget to update the fvars field of the environment.

Write the function

Notion: field and function of the same name

The field fvars of an environment and the function fvars on types do not conflict: env.fvars is the field, fvars t the function. The same holds for the field typ of a scheme and the type typ.

Hint: free variables recorded earlier

With x : δ in the environment, the set holds δ. If unification then defines δ := ε → int, the variable free in the environment is ε, and the set still holds δ.

Applying fvars (Tvar v) to each variable v of the set gives the variables free now.

which adds an entry to a typing environment while generalizing its type with respect to all its free type variables that do not appear in the environment (it will be used when typing a let).

Write the function

Hint: generalization

The quantified variables are the free variables of the type minus those free in the environment: ftv(τ) ∖ ftv(Γ).

A variable free in the environment belongs to the type of a parameter of an enclosing fun, and has to be the same type at all its uses: it stays out.

which returns the type associated with an identifier in an environment, after replacing all variables of the corresponding scheme by fresh type variables. Careful: there may be several occurrences of the same variable in the type, and of course they must all be replaced by the same fresh variable. Hint: we can introduce a module module Vmap = Map.Make(V) and use a value of type tvar Vmap.t to represent this substitution.

Hint: instantiation

A substitution is built first, with one fresh variable for each quantified variable; it is then applied to the whole type. Two occurrences of α are looked up in the same substitution and get the same fresh variable.

A variable absent from the substitution is not quantified and stays as it is. Each call builds new variables: two uses of an identifier get two independent copies of its type.

Question 5. Algorithm W

We are given the following type for mini-ML expressions:

Write the function

Notion: three kinds of variable

A variable of the mini-ML program is Var "x": a string, the key of Smap. A type variable is Tvar v: a record with an id. The variables of the checker itself are those of OCaml: env, t1, v.

A string constant is a pattern: Op "+" matches that operator only.

implementing algorithm W. For operators (Op), we can restrict ourselves to Op "+" of type int * int -> int.

To test, we will use the following function

Concept: shadowing

A second let of the same name defines a new variable, which hides the first in what follows; the first is not changed, and what was defined with it still sees it. let env = add … env in builds an extended environment under the same name, for the rest of that case only.

Hint: parameter of a function

The type of the parameter is not known when fun x -> e is entered: x gets a fresh variable α, added without generalization, and typing the body defines α as far as the body constrains it. The result is α → τ.

Hint: fresh variable for the result of an application

In e1 e2, with τ1 the type of e1 and τ2 the type of e2, τ1 has to be an arrow from τ2 to a result that is not known. A fresh variable α stands for it: unifying τ1 with τ2 → α finds it, and α is the type of the application.

Hint: generalization at let only

In let x = e1 in e2 the type of e1 is generalized before e2 is typed, so x has a scheme and each use takes a new instance. The parameter of a fun has one type.

That is why the first program below is accepted and the second rejected.

Notion: numbers of the type variables

A type variable is printed with its number, '12. The number depends on how many variables were created before: it changes as soon as a test is added or moved. A test on a polymorphic type compares the variables with V.equal and never compares a number with a fixed value.
